title: Discontinuous orbital angular momentum metasurface holography

paper_content.abstract: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing holography has emerged as a pivotal technology for high-capacity optical communication, encryption and display, but it requires multiple inputs for decoding and its security remains constrained due to the rotational symmetry of topological charge (TC) distribution in conventional OAM modes. Here, we introduce a general paradigm of OAM multiplexing holography that enables multi-channel holographic encoding using a single incident light. Our methodology leverages a discontinuous OAM with a spatially varying TC across the azimuth, which breaks the rotational symmetry and imposes angular selectivity for information retrieval. Notably, by rationally designing the TC distribution, the discontinuous OAM exhibits self-orthogonality at different rotation angles, laying the foundation for multiplexed holography. A modified weighted Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm is developed to calculate the holographic phase profile, which can then be encoded onto a pure geometry-phase metasurface. By further integrating different pairs of discontinuous OAMs, we successfully expand the channel capacity for holographic multiplexing, significantly advancing high-security and high-capacity optical information encryption. Our work establishes discontinuous OAM as a versatile platform for secure optical communications, high-density data storage, and dynamic holographic displays, bridging the gap between structured light manipulation and cryptographic robustness.
paper_content.introduction:
Metasurfaces, composed of sub-wavelength artificial structure arrays, have made a profound impact on the fields of optics and photonics due to their exceptional performance, such as compact size and high resolution, ushering optical components into the era of planar optics. They possess unprecedented ability to manipulate various degrees of freedom, such as phase1–6, amplitude5,6, and polarization7,8, through intense light–matter interactions9–11. This capability enables metasurfaces to facilitate advanced multiplexing applications, particularly in metasurface holography, also referred to as meta-hologram12–14.

Recently, a variety of multiplexing techniques for metasurface holography have been explored, including polarization multiplexing15–17, wavelength multiplexing18–20, incident angle-multiplexing21–23, and spatial multiplexing24,25. Among these, orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing has emerged as an especially promising technique26–29, as OAM offers theoretically unlimited orthogonal channels. This enables the multiplexing of a large number of OAM-dependent information channels within a single meta-hologram30–40. However, conventional OAM-multiplexing holography relies on azimuthally symmetric OAM encoding. By randomly inputting regular OAM states, the encoded information can be easily retrieved, thereby significantly compromising the security of the information. In addition, each channel is encoded with a single constant topological charge (TC) of OAM, which inevitably requires different input vortex beams with distinct TCs of OAM to decode separate holographic images, thereby complicating the generation of multiple holographic channels.

Here, we propose a general method for OAM multiplexing holography using a single input beam that is azimuthally encoded with discontinuous TCs of OAM. Our methodology relies on the fact that the discontinuous arrangement of TC breaks the rotational symmetry of the OAM mode, laying the foundation to encode multiple holographic channels by simply rotating the single input beam. We prove that by strategically arranging the azimuthally distributed TCs, the discontinuous OAM exhibits self-orthogonality at different rotation angles, ensuring minimal cross-talk between channels. Additionally, various discontinuous OAMs can be multiplexed on a single device, further enhancing the holographic channels. To achieve this, a modified weighted Gerchberg–Saxton (WGS) algorithm is introduced for the generation of holographic phase information, which is then encoded in a pure geometry-phase metasurface. Notably, the encrypted holographic images using the discontinuous OAM cannot be decrypted by illuminating with conventional continuous OAM, significantly enhancing the security of the information. Our work paves the way for high-capacity and high-security information transfer and optical networks, addressing the escalating demands of optical and quantum communications, as well as big-data photonics.
paper_content.results:
Design principle of discontinuous OAM holography
The design principle of discontinuous OAM metasurface holography is illustrated in Fig. 1. In conventional OAM holography, the illuminated OAM mode exhibits rotational symmetry due to the constant TC, resulting in an output holographic image that remains invariant regardless of the incident beam’s rotation angle as shown in Fig. 1a. In contrast, the proposed discontinuous OAM holography leverages a rotational symmetry broken OAM mode, featuring azimuthally encoded TCs, which exhibit azimuth-dependent channel selectivity as shown in Fig. 1b. The encoded holographic image can only be reconstructed when the azimuth of the incident OAM mode aligns precisely with the encoded phase. This enables multiple holographic images to be encoded at different rotation angles of the incident OAM mode, significantly enhancing the multiplexing channel numbers under single beam illumination. Our discontinuous OAM holography offers a security enhancement of at least 7 orders of magnitude compared to traditional OAM holographic encryption (see more details in Supplementary Note 1). Specifically, we encode distinct TCs across varying azimuth, with each TC value assigned to a specific angular region defined as l(θ). Switching between multiple independent channels—from image “A” to “D”—can be achieved by rotating the input OAM mode. Compared to constant OAM, discontinuous OAM generates multimodal spectral interference due to its azimuthal phase partitioning. This inherent complexity fundamentally resists detection and decryption through spiral spectrum analysis. Consequently, any attempt to reconstruct the encrypted hologram via exhaustive constant OAM modes fails to achieve meaningful reconstruction.

To investigate the optical properties of discontinuous OAM, we design a dual-partition OAM by evenly dividing the azimuth into two regions, each encoded with distinct TCs. Generally, the electric field distribution of the output beam by illuminating the discontinuous OAM can be expressed as41,

E(r,ϕ) = C \sum_{j=-1}^{0} a_j e^{i(l+j)(ϕ∓π/2)} \int J_{l+j}(krρ/f) ρ dρ (1)

where i^2 = −1, r and ϕ are the polar coordinates on the output image plane, ρ is the radial coordinates on the metasurface plane, f is the focal length, λ is the operating wavelength, k = 2π/λ is the wave-vector, a_j is the coefficient related to the rectangular function, l denotes the number of TC, J(·) is the Bessel function, C is a constant.

In the example illustrated in Fig. 1c, the azimuthal plane is divided into two distinct regions (top-left panel of Fig. 1c: the brown segment encodes a negative TC of l = −10, while the blue segment encodes a positive TC of l = 10). The electric field distribution of the output light undergoes a characteristic 90° rotation relative to the encoded phase pattern (bottom-left panel of Fig. 1c), with the rotation direction governed by the sign of TC (see more details of the rotation rules in Supplementary Note 2 and Fig. S2). Specifically, a negative TC induces a −90° rotation of the spatial electric field distribution, whereas a positive TC generates a +90° rotation. Therefore, for the dual-partition discontinuous OAM with opposite sign of TCs, the spatial electric field distributions of the two partitioned regions overlap coherently in free space as shown in the bottom-left panel of Fig. 1c, which can be described as,

E ∝ cos(10ϕ), ϕ ∈ [π/2, 3π/2] (2)

However, the phase discontinuity between the two regions and the mismatch in TC at the partitioned boundaries introduce a half-period gap in the petal pattern, breaking the rotational symmetry and resulting in an asymmetric intensity profile.

We further investigate the self-orthogonality of the discontinuous OAM mode at different rotation angles. As illustrated in Fig. 1c, d, two sets of multiplexing configurations with different relative rotation angles—Multiplexing Mode 1 and Multiplexing Mode 2 are analyzed. In Mode 1, the two discontinuous OAMs (first two columns of Fig. 1c) exhibit a relative rotation angle of 180°, showing no overlap in their azimuthal TC distribution, thereby ensuring complete orthogonality. This orthogonality is also manifested in real space as the beam propagates (bottom panel of Fig. 1c). Each discontinuous OAM contributes symmetrically to half of the ring pattern, and their superposition yields a uniform annular intensity profile. In contrast, Mode 2 introduces a 90° azimuthal shift between the two OAMs, showing partial overlap of the TC distribution (red dashed box in the top panel of Fig. 1d), which leads to crosstalk in the spatial electric field distributions. This overlap breaks orthogonality, and the superposition in real space generates an interference pattern with crosstalk. Figure 1e quantifies the orthogonality of the two modes (see calculation details in Supplementary Notes 3 and 4), highlighting the superior orthogonality of Mode 1 compared to Mode 2. As a result, Mode 1 is suitable for multiplexing due to its complete orthogonality. These findings underscore the critical role of spatially non-overlapping discontinuous OAM designs in achieving high-fidelity multiplexing holography.

Design processes of discontinuous OAM holography
The algorithm process for the discontinuous OAM multiplexing holography is shown in Fig. 2a. The holographic phase information for different channels is first generated from sampled images using a WGS algorithm (see details in Supplementary Note 5). The phase is subsequently superimposed with the discontinuous OAM at different rotation angles. The final phase profile is obtained by superimposing all holographic channels, leading to multi-channel OAM holography on a single phase profile. The metasurface is composed of subwavelength TiO2 nanopillar arrays with a fixed height of 600 nm on a SiO2 substrate. These nanopillars are designed as half-waveplates to convert the handedness of circular polarized (CP) light and impose a geometry phase when the nanopillars are rotated at various angles. Therefore, the final phase profile of the discontinuous OAM holography can be encoded pixel by pixel in the geometry-phase metasurface. The width and length of the nanopillars are chosen as L1 = 100 nm and L2 = 290 nm, showing optimized CP conversion efficiency in the visible range (see more details in Supplementary Note 6). The experimental optical setup (see more details in the “Methods” section) and the scanning electron microscopic image of the fabricated metasurface are illustrated in Fig. 2b, c, respectively.

Experiments of single-discontinuous-OAM multiplexing holography
Figure 3a, b show the decoded holograms of two discontinuous OAM multiplexing modes, with simulation results in the second row and experimental results in the third row. In Mode 1, when two discontinuous OAM beams with rotation angles of 0° and 180° are illuminated, a minimal crosstalk between the two images is observed due to their complete orthogonality as discussed in Fig. 1c, and near-perfect Gaussian spot distribution are obtained as shown in the first two columns of Fig. 3a. It should be noted that slight crosstalk between the two channels appears in the experimental results due to fabrication errors. When illuminated by a plane wave, as shown in the third column of Fig. 3a, the two images of “0” and “1” do not overlap, each showing opposite half-ring vortices (see the zoomed-in figures in the bottom-right panel of Fig. 3a): Image “0” shows a right-half vortex, while Image “1” shows a left-half vortex, with their opening directions matching those in Fig. 1c. The overlapping regions of Image “0” and “1” produce a seamless annular “petal-like” intensity profile formed by their coherent superposition. In contrast, Mode 2, with a relative rotation angle of 90° between the two discontinuous incident OAMs, suffers from non-orthogonality as discussed in Fig. 1d, leading to significant crosstalk that degrades image quality as shown in the first two columns of Fig. 3b. Although the decoded images still yield a Gaussian-like spot distribution, the non-overlapping regions for Image “0” retain the right-half vortex, while Image “1” displays a top-half vortex. As a result, under plane wave illumination, the overlapping regions generate an incomplete three-quarter annular pattern.

To quantify the imaging fidelity, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is calculated for both modes as shown in Fig. 3c. It is evident that Mode 1 achieves a higher SNR than Mode 2. Figure 3d further demonstrates the azimuth sensitivity of discontinuous OAM. Rotating the incident beam reduces the SNR of the original channel while progressively activating the complementary channel (see more details in Supplementary Note 4). Specifically, at a 0° rotation, Image “0” is fully decoded, while at a 180° rotation, Image “1” is fully decoded, highlighting the rotation-angle selectivity of the incident beam inherent in the discontinuous OAM encoding. This behavior underscores the multidimensional security and dynamic channel-switching capabilities enabled by discontinuous OAM holography.

To validate the scalability of our method, a four-channel discontinuous OAM holography is designed as shown in Fig. 4, where distinct information channels are selectively activated by rotating the incident discontinuous OAM beam with 90° intervals. Figure 4a illustrates the rotational encoding scheme, and Fig. 4b quantifies the SNR of the decoded images across the four channels as a function of rotation angle. At 0°, 90°, 180°, and 270° rotations, the SNR of the decoded images “A”, “B”, “C”, and “D” are normalized to 1, respectively, with the maximal SNR occurring at these angles, while intermediate angles exhibit severe crosstalk. Both simulated (Fig. 4c) and experimental results (Fig. 4d) confirm the azimuth selectivity. The reconstructed patterns at intermediate angles, characterized by hybrid intensity profiles, are detailed in Supplementary Note 7.

Experiments of multiple polarization and discontinuous-OAM hybrid multiplexing holography
To further expand multiplexing dimensions and enhance channel capacity, we incorporated polarization and multiple pairs of discontinuous OAMs as an additional degree of freedom. Specifically, by integrating two pairs of discontinuous OAM modes with two orthogonal polarization states, we have designed an eight-channel metasurface multiplexed holography in Fig. 5. For left-circularly polarized (LCP) light, two pairs of orthogonal discontinuous OAM modes l = ±15, l = ±22 are employed to encode four distinct images. Similarly, for right-circularly polarized (RCP) light, the set of OAM modes l = ±15, l = ±10 encodes another four independent images. The superimposed phase of LCP light denoted by σ+ is inverted due to the opposite phase response between RCP and LCP, as shown in Fig. 5a. Consequently, the phase profile can be expressed as,

φ = arg [\sum_{n=1}^{N} e^{i(φ_n^{σ-} + ϕ_n^{r1})} + \sum_{m=1}^{M} e^{i(φ_m^{σ+} + ϕ_m^{r2})}] (3)

where channel n = 1, 2, ..., N, with N being the channel number of discontinuous OAM holography for RCP, m = 1, 2, ..., M, with M being the channel number of discontinuous OAM holography for LCP, σ- and σ+ denote RCP and LCP, respectively, φ_n^σ and φ_m^σ is the calculated phase by the WGS algorithm. The phase of discontinuous OAM ϕ_n^r1 and ϕ_n^r2 is then added to the holographic phase.

The demonstration of a geometry-phase metasurface supporting the polarization-discontinuous OAM hybrid encoding is based on a non-interleaved method35. We integrated two-channel discontinuous OAM encoding with polarization multiplexing. When illuminated with an LCP beam carrying TC of l = ±15, the letter “M” is successfully decoded. When the metasurface is rotated by 180°, the decoded image switches from letter “M” to letter “E”, demonstrating dynamic channel switching through angular control as shown in Fig. 5b. Similarly, when illuminated with LCP beam carrying l = ±22, the letter “T” is decoded, and a 180° rotation of the metasurface enables switching from “T” to “A”. For RCP beam illumination, four distinct images “1”, “2”, “3”, and “4” can likewise be decoded as shown in Fig. 5c, demonstrating polarization multiplexing capability.

The reconstructed images exhibit near-perfect Gaussian spot profiles. The polarization selectivity and azimuthal selectivity of discontinuous OAM ensure that each channel is activated only when the polarization and the alignment of the incident beam match the encoded phase profile, thereby enabling dynamic, high-capacity, and high-security holography with cryptographic robustness. Notably, the numerals and letters in all the holographic images shown in Figs. 3–5 are designed in the same spatial position, yet exhibit almost no crosstalk between different channels.
paper_content.methods:
Sample fabrication
The metasurface samples are prepared using electron beam lithography (EBL). First, a 600 nm-thick titanium dioxide (TiO2) film is deposited on a silicon dioxide (SiO2) substrate by sputtering evaporation. A polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) layer is evenly spin-coated onto the TiO2 film. After EBL, the PMMA resist is developed, and a Cr film is deposited on the PMMA using electron beam evaporation (EBE). The undeveloped PMMA is removed, and the TiO2 is etched using reactive ion etching. The process end with the removal of the Cr mask by chemical etching.

Optical setup
The experimental optical setup for the discontinuous OAM holography is shown in Fig. 2b. The laser from a supercontinuum laser source (SC-PRO, Wuhan Yangtze Soton Laser Co., Ltd., 430–2400 nm) filtered by an acousto-optic tunable filter (AOTF, Wuhan Yangtze Soton Laser Co., Ltd., 400–2000 nm) is initially expand the beam through the objective lens (L1, NA = 0.65) and then directed through a beam splitter, projected perpendicularly onto a spatial light modulator (SLM, HOLOEYE PLUTO-2.1-NIR−135, German). This is to generate a vertically emitted discontinuous OAM beam. Then, lens L2 (f = 150 mm), lens L3 (f = 50 mm), and lens L4 (f = 75 mm) are used to focus the discontinuous OAM onto the metasurface. A set of polarizer and quarter-wave plate is used to convert the polarization of the incident beam from linear polarization to LCP light. A scientific complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor camera (Dhyana 400BSI V2, Tucsen, China) is used to extract the holographic images.

Data availability
The data that support the figures and other findings of this study are available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request.

The code that support the figures and other findings of this study is available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors of manuscript NCOMMS-25-25303 proposed and demonstrated a novel kind of metasurface holography based
on discontinuous orbital angular momentum (OAM). This discontinuous OAM has a spatially varying TC across the
azimuthal angle, and thus breaks the rotational symmetry of the beam for information retrieval. Generally, this study
differentiates itself from traditional OAM-based holographic approaches through the employment of discontinuous OAM
modes. However, after careful evaluation, I am currently hesitant to recommend this study, based on the following reasons.
1. Their proposal provides significance such as using a single beam in information retrieval. However, this method may also
bring along limitations, such as extra complexities in precisely controlling the rotation angle and spatial position of the input
beam in retrieving the information.
2. The conventional OAM holography has significant merit of information encryption. I’m doubt of the scenarios with
necessity to further enhance the security of the information, especially at the cost of adding extra complexity in information
retrieval, because the authors said ‘any deviation in the rotation angle, or illumination with conventional constant OAM, will
trigger severe inter-channel crosstalk,’.
3. In the text, the authors mentioned that ‘We prove that by strategically arranging the azimuthally distributed TCs, the
discontinuous OAM exhibits self-orthogonality at different rotation angles, ensuring minimal cross-talk between channels.’
The comparison of cross-talk with the conventional metasurface holography and state-of-the-art holography techniques with
small cross-talk has not been fully discussed.
4. The authors mentioned that ‘This enables multiple holographic images to be encoded at different rotation angles of the
incident OAM mode, significantly enhancing the multiplexing channel numbers under single beam illumination.’ However, in
the experiment, the detail of how to precisely control the rotation angle in coding and decoding has not been fully discussed.
5. Does the phase distribution necessarily require topological charges with opposite signs, or could the same functionality
be achieved using same-sign charges with discontinuous phase profiles (such as TC=1, 2, 3, 4)?
6. Are the light spots at the letter edges in the experimental optical field of Figure 4d manually traced? If so, this image
processing procedure should be explicitly declared in the main text.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript proposes a new paradigm of metasurface holography based on discontinuous orbital angular momentum
(OAM), which enables multi-channel holographic encoding under a single incident beam by breaking the rotational
symmetry of conventional OAM modes. The work demonstrates certain innovation in enhancing optical information security
and capacity, particularly in the design and application of spatially varying topological charge (TC) distributions. However,
considering the high academic standards and scientific rigor expected by Nature Communications, the current manuscript
still exhibits certain shortcomings in theoretical depth, experimental validation, and practical feasibility, falling short of the
publication threshold. To improve the overall quality of the manuscript, the authors are advised to systematically address the
following key issues.
First, traditional OAM multiplexing holography has shown great potential in high-capacity communication due to its
propagation-invariant and stable characteristics. However, the proposed discontinuous OAM mode, while breaking the
central symmetry, may adversely affect the beam’s transmission properties. For example, it remains insufficiently verified
whether the structural integrity of the beam can be preserved after transmission through optical fibers (such as few-mode or
ring-core fibers) or through free space. Therefore, the application prospects emphasized in the manuscript require further
substantiation, and it is recommended that the authors supplement the manuscript with relevant experimental or simulation-
based analyses of transmission performance.
Second, although the authors claim that the method effectively enhances the capacity of encryption channels, the
experimental results presented in the manuscript demonstrate only a limited number of multiplexed channels—just a few in
total. In contrast, traditional OAM holography has already achieved tens or even hundreds of multiplexed channels, with
some metasurface-based schemes reaching over ten channels. As such, the advantage of the current approach in terms of
capacity enhancement is not yet clearly demonstrated. The authors are encouraged to more explicitly clarify the core
competitiveness of their method compared to traditional techniques and to further validate its potential by expanding the
number of channels or integrating additional degrees of freedom.
Third, although conventional centrally symmetric OAM multiplexing holography imposes certain alignment requirements on
the devices, its inherent symmetry to some extent reduces the difficulty of alignment. After breaking this symmetry, however,
the precision required for alignment may significantly increase, especially when rotational operations are introduced, where
accurate centering becomes critical to decoding performance. The manuscript should therefore include a discussion on
alignment error tolerance and assess its impact on overall system performance.
Fourth, while the manuscript emphasizes the advantage of discontinuous OAM in resisting spiral spectrum analysis, it lacks
thorough security analysis under more complex attack scenarios, such as phase reconstruction based on machine learning
or partial information leakage. It is recommended that the authors supplement the manuscript with corresponding
experimental or simulation data to verify the system’s robustness under different attack models and explore potential
mechanisms for enhancing security.
Finally, the manuscript mentions the possibility of further expanding channel capacity by integrating other degrees of
freedom, such as polarization and wavelength. However, specific technical pathways and challenges have not been
adequately addressed, especially regarding possible crosstalk between different degrees of freedom. It is suggested that the
authors include preliminary experimental or simulation results on multi-degree-of-freedom multiplexing—for instance,
validating the feasibility of combined polarization-OAM encoding—and analyze the coupling mechanisms between different
degrees of freedom (e.g., polarization-dependent phase modulation), proposing effective decoupling strategies to
demonstrate the future potential of this technology in high-dimensional multiplexing.
In summary, this manuscript presents a forward-looking technical concept, but there remains significant room for
improvement in terms of theoretical completeness, depth of experimental validation, and practical feasibility. If the authors
can systematically revise and enhance the manuscript in response to the above-mentioned concerns, the scientific value
and engineering relevance of the work could be substantially strengthened, making it a stronger candidate for
reconsideration for publication.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript presents a novel approach for multi-channel holographic imaging by encoding multiple holographic images
into a single metasurface and decoding them using structured light generated by a spatial light modulator (SLM).
Compared to conventional methods—where a single orbital angular momentum (OAM) pattern generated by the SLM typically decodes
only one hologram—this work utilizes discontinuous OAM beams with spatially separated topological charges. This design
allows different holographic images to be selectively decoded by rotating the input beam, thereby enabling dynamic and
secure multiplexing. Overall, this work demonstrates an innovative and technically sound advancement in the areas of OAM
optics, holography, cryptographic imaging, and multifunctional metasurface design. Considering the following technical
issues, I believe the manuscript is suitable for publication in Nature Communications after minor revision.
1. In the manuscript, does Equation (2) specifically refer to the angular range [π/2, 3π/2]? If so, would it be more appropriate
to explicitly label this range near the equation for clarity? Additionally, I reviewed Supporting Information Equation (6), but I
couldn’t clearly see how this expression explains why the electric field is nearly zero in the angular range [-π/2, π/2]. Why
the “petal-like” intensity pattern only appears on the left side? Could the authors clarify how this behavior is captured by Eq.
(6), or whether any assumptions or approximations are involved?
2. In Figures 1(c) and 1(d), the bottom panels are labeled as "electric field distributions." However, based on the visual
patterns, they appear to represent intensity profiles rather than complex field amplitudes. Should these be labeled as
“intensity” instead of “electric field” for accuracy and clarity?
3. I recommend that the authors consider adding a colorbar next to the phase distributions in Figure 1 of the main text for
clarity. Additionally, I noticed a potential inconsistency in the phase color mapping. In Figure 1c, the brown-colored phase
progresses from dark brown to white as the azimuthal angle increases, which corresponds to a positive topological charge
(ℓ=+10). However, in the brown segment of Figure 2a, the same color progression—from dark brown to white with increasing
azimuth—appears to represent a negative topological charge (ℓ=−10). For clarity and consistency, I suggest the authors
ensure that the color mapping of phase is consistently represented throughout the figures, especially for readers interpreting
the sign of the OAM from the color gradient.
4. While Supplementary Note 3 provides insight into the orthogonality behavior via inner product analysis, it would be
helpful if the authors could clarify the specific method used to compute the SNR values shown in Figures 3c and 3d—such
as how the signal and noise regions are defined, and whether any averaging or normalization is applied. In particular, the
near-perfect Gaussian spot distribution appears only when angular orthogonality is achieved. However, even in the absence
of orthogonality, there is still observable power forming a petal-like intensity pattern. This raises the question of how exactly
the SNR and orthogonality are defined and processed in the data analysis.
5. In Figure 2a, I noticed that the phase distributions corresponding to images B and C appear highly similar. Since the
authors mention that the meta-atoms are based on geometric phase, and the Methods section only specifies LCP
illumination, the polarization state of the incident light is not fully described throughout the manuscript. Could the authors
clarify whether different circular polarizations (e.g., LCP vs. RCP) were used to access additional holographic channels?
If so, it would be helpful to elaborate on the polarization dependence and specify which channels were designed for which
incident polarization state.
6. In Figure 5b, the experimental holographic images for the six-channel configuration appear noticeably clearer than those
in the four-channel case shown in Figure 4d. Interestingly, in the six-channel experiment, each decoded holographic image
is encoded using two OAM values (i.e., a pair of ±ℓ). Does this suggest that encoding each holographic image with a pair of
OAM values inherently leads to better reconstruction quality? It would also be helpful if the authors could provide
quantitative metrics (e.g., SNR) for the six-channel case to facilitate a direct comparison with the four-channel results.

Comment 2: This manuscript proposes a new paradigm of metasurface holography
based on discontinuous orbital angular momentum (OAM), which enables multi-
channel holographic encoding under a single incident beam by breaking the rotational
symmetry of conventional OAM modes. The work demonstrates certain innovation in
enhancing optical information security and capacity, particularly in the design and
application of spatially varying topological charge (TC) distributions. However,
considering the high academic standards and scientific rigor expected by Nature
Communications, the current manuscript still exhibits certain shortcomings in
theoretical depth, experimental validation, and practical feasibility, falling short of the
publication threshold. To improve the overall quality of the manuscript, the authors are
advised to systematically address the following key issues.
Response 2: We would like to thank the reviewer for the affirmation of the novelty of
our work. We are happy to address all the concerns raised by the reviewer.
Comment 2.1: First, traditional OAM multiplexing holography has shown great
potential in high-capacity communication due to its propagation-invariant and stable
characteristics. However, the proposed discontinuous OAM mode, while breaking the
central symmetry, may adversely affect the beam’s transmission properties. For
example, it remains insufficiently verified whether the structural integrity of the beam
can be preserved after transmission through optical fibers (such as few-mode or ring-
core fibers) or through free space. Therefore, the application prospects emphasized in
the manuscript require further substantiation, and it is recommended that the authors
supplement the manuscript with relevant experimental or simulation-based analyses of
transmission performance.
Response 2.1: The authors thank the reviewer for this point. Taking two-channel
discontinuous OAM as an example. Within the oresnel diffraction regime, a vortex
beam carrying half-integer OAM exhibits a semi-vortex morphology. The opening
direction of this semi-vortex rotates with propagation distance until attaining a 90°
phase offset relative to its initial state. The rotation direction is determined by the sign
of the TC as explained in Supplementary Note 2. The discontinuous OAM proposed
in this manuscript arises from the superposition of two such semi-vortices, which
generate a petal-like beam profile. After the oresnel diffraction regime, i.e., in the far
field, the discontinuous OAM beam propagates stable in free space as shown in Fig.
S21.

Comment 2.2: Second, although the authors claim that the method effectively enhances

Response 2.2: The authors thank the reviewer for this valuable point. Conventional
OAM metasurface holography achieving tens or hundreds of multiplexed channels
relies on complex-amplitude metasurfaces. Compared to phase-only metasurfaces,
complex-amplitude designs exhibit lower crosstalk and higher image fidelity. However,
due to fabrication constraints in realizing complex-amplitude structures in our
laboratory, we adopted a phase-only metasurface approach utilizing Pancharatnam-
Berry (PB) phase for multi-channel multiplexing. In the previous paper presented by
Ren Haoran et al. (Nat. Commun., 10, 2986, 2019), they demonstrated ten-channel
phase-only OAM holography in simulations. oor comparison, we present both
simulation and experimental results for ten-channel discontinuous OAM holography.
In Fig. S17 and Fig. S18, we show that both eight-channel and ten-channel
discontinuous OAM holography can be successfully achieved.
The key advantage over discontinuous OAM holography lies in enabling channel
switching through metasurface rotation under single-beam illumination, which is an
unattainable feature in traditional systems. Moreover, it offers enhanced security as
decoding requires precise knowledge of both the encoded azimuthal sectors and their
corresponding TC.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing holography has emerged as a pivotal technology for high-capacity optical communication, encryption and display, but it requires multiple inputs for decoding and its security remains constrained due to the rotational symmetry of topological charge (TC) distribution in conventional OAM modes. Here, we introduce a general paradigm of OAM multiplexing holography that enables multi-channel holographic encoding using a single incident light. Our methodology leverages a discontinuous OAM with a spatially varying TC across the azimuth, which breaks the rotational symmetry and imposes angular selectivity for information retrieval. Notably, by rationally designing the TC distribution, the discontinuous OAM exhibits self-orthogonality at different rotation angles, laying the foundation for multiplexed holography. A modified weighted Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm is developed to calculate the holographic phase profile, which can then be encoded onto a pure geometry-phase metasurface. By further integrating different pairs of discontinuous OAMs, we successfully expand the channel capacity for holographic multiplexing, significantly advancing high-security and high-capacity optical information encryption. Our work establishes discontinuous OAM as a versatile platform for secure optical communications, high-density data storage, and dynamic holographic displays, bridging the gap between structured light manipulation and cryptographic robustness.

---

## Introduction

Metasurfaces, composed of sub-wavelength artificial structure arrays, have made a profound impact on the fields of optics and photonics due to their exceptional performance, such as compact size and high resolution, ushering optical components into the era of planar optics. They possess unprecedented ability to manipulate various degrees of freedom, such as phase1–6, amplitude5,6, and polarization7,8, through intense light–matter interactions9–11. This capability enables metasurfaces to facilitate advanced multiplexing applications, particularly in metasurface holography, also referred to as meta-hologram12–14.

Recently, a variety of multiplexing techniques for metasurface holography have been explored, including polarization multiplexing15–17, wavelength multiplexing18–20, incident angle-multiplexing21–23, and spatial multiplexing24,25. Among these, orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing has emerged as an especially promising technique26–29, as OAM offers theoretically unlimited orthogonal channels. This enables the multiplexing of a large number of OAM-dependent information channels within a single meta-hologram30–40. However, conventional OAM-multiplexing holography relies on azimuthally symmetric OAM encoding. By randomly inputting regular OAM states, the encoded information can be easily retrieved, thereby significantly compromising the security of the information. In addition, each channel is encoded with a single constant topological charge (TC) of OAM, which inevitably requires different input vortex beams with distinct TCs of OAM to decode separate holographic images, thereby complicating the generation of multiple holographic channels.

Here, we propose a general method for OAM multiplexing holography using a single input beam that is azimuthally encoded with discontinuous TCs of OAM. Our methodology relies on the fact that the discontinuous arrangement of TC breaks the rotational symmetry of the OAM mode, laying the foundation to encode multiple holographic channels by simply rotating the single input beam. We prove that by strategically arranging the azimuthally distributed TCs, the discontinuous OAM exhibits self-orthogonality at different rotation angles, ensuring minimal cross-talk between channels. Additionally, various discontinuous OAMs can be multiplexed on a single device, further enhancing the holographic channels. To achieve this, a modified weighted Gerchberg–Saxton (WGS) algorithm is introduced for the generation of holographic phase information, which is then encoded in a pure geometry-phase metasurface. Notably, the encrypted holographic images using the discontinuous OAM cannot be decrypted by illuminating with conventional continuous OAM, significantly enhancing the security of the information. Our work paves the way for high-capacity and high-security information transfer and optical networks, addressing the escalating demands of optical and quantum communications, as well as big-data photonics.

---

## Results

Design principle of discontinuous OAM holography
The design principle of discontinuous OAM metasurface holography is illustrated in Fig. 1. In conventional OAM holography, the illuminated OAM mode exhibits rotational symmetry due to the constant TC, resulting in an output holographic image that remains invariant regardless of the incident beam’s rotation angle as shown in Fig. 1a. In contrast, the proposed discontinuous OAM holography leverages a rotational symmetry broken OAM mode, featuring azimuthally encoded TCs, which exhibit azimuth-dependent channel selectivity as shown in Fig. 1b. The encoded holographic image can only be reconstructed when the azimuth of the incident OAM mode aligns precisely with the encoded phase. This enables multiple holographic images to be encoded at different rotation angles of the incident OAM mode, significantly enhancing the multiplexing channel numbers under single beam illumination. Our discontinuous OAM holography offers a security enhancement of at least 7 orders of magnitude compared to traditional OAM holographic encryption (see more details in Supplementary Note 1). Specifically, we encode distinct TCs across varying azimuth, with each TC value assigned to a specific angular region defined as l(θ). Switching between multiple independent channels—from image “A” to “D”—can be achieved by rotating the input OAM mode. Compared to constant OAM, discontinuous OAM generates multimodal spectral interference due to its azimuthal phase partitioning. This inherent complexity fundamentally resists detection and decryption through spiral spectrum analysis. Consequently, any attempt to reconstruct the encrypted hologram via exhaustive constant OAM modes fails to achieve meaningful reconstruction.

To investigate the optical properties of discontinuous OAM, we design a dual-partition OAM by evenly dividing the azimuth into two regions, each encoded with distinct TCs. Generally, the electric field distribution of the output beam by illuminating the discontinuous OAM can be expressed as41,

E(r,ϕ) = C \sum_{j=-1}^{0} a_j e^{i(l+j)(ϕ∓π/2)} \int J_{l+j}(krρ/f) ρ dρ (1)

where i^2 = −1, r and ϕ are the polar coordinates on the output image plane, ρ is the radial coordinates on the metasurface plane, f is the focal length, λ is the operating wavelength, k = 2π/λ is the wave-vector, a_j is the coefficient related to the rectangular function, l denotes the number of TC, J(·) is the Bessel function, C is a constant.

In the example illustrated in Fig. 1c, the azimuthal plane is divided into two distinct regions (top-left panel of Fig. 1c: the brown segment encodes a negative TC of l = −10, while the blue segment encodes a positive TC of l = 10). The electric field distribution of the output light undergoes a characteristic 90° rotation relative to the encoded phase pattern (bottom-left panel of Fig. 1c), with the rotation direction governed by the sign of TC (see more details of the rotation rules in Supplementary Note 2 and Fig. S2). Specifically, a negative TC induces a −90° rotation of the spatial electric field distribution, whereas a positive TC generates a +90° rotation. Therefore, for the dual-partition discontinuous OAM with opposite sign of TCs, the spatial electric field distributions of the two partitioned regions overlap coherently in free space as shown in the bottom-left panel of Fig. 1c, which can be described as,

E ∝ cos(10ϕ), ϕ ∈ [π/2, 3π/2] (2)

However, the phase discontinuity between the two regions and the mismatch in TC at the partitioned boundaries introduce a half-period gap in the petal pattern, breaking the rotational symmetry and resulting in an asymmetric intensity profile.

We further investigate the self-orthogonality of the discontinuous OAM mode at different rotation angles. As illustrated in Fig. 1c, d, two sets of multiplexing configurations with different relative rotation angles—Multiplexing Mode 1 and Multiplexing Mode 2 are analyzed. In Mode 1, the two discontinuous OAMs (first two columns of Fig. 1c) exhibit a relative rotation angle of 180°, showing no overlap in their azimuthal TC distribution, thereby ensuring complete orthogonality. This orthogonality is also manifested in real space as the beam propagates (bottom panel of Fig. 1c). Each discontinuous OAM contributes symmetrically to half of the ring pattern, and their superposition yields a uniform annular intensity profile. In contrast, Mode 2 introduces a 90° azimuthal shift between the two OAMs, showing partial overlap of the TC distribution (red dashed box in the top panel of Fig. 1d), which leads to crosstalk in the spatial electric field distributions. This overlap breaks orthogonality, and the superposition in real space generates an interference pattern with crosstalk. Figure 1e quantifies the orthogonality of the two modes (see calculation details in Supplementary Notes 3 and 4), highlighting the superior orthogonality of Mode 1 compared to Mode 2. As a result, Mode 1 is suitable for multiplexing due to its complete orthogonality. These findings underscore the critical role of spatially non-overlapping discontinuous OAM designs in achieving high-fidelity multiplexing holography.

Design processes of discontinuous OAM holography
The algorithm process for the discontinuous OAM multiplexing holography is shown in Fig. 2a. The holographic phase information for different channels is first generated from sampled images using a WGS algorithm (see details in Supplementary Note 5). The phase is subsequently superimposed with the discontinuous OAM at different rotation angles. The final phase profile is obtained by superimposing all holographic channels, leading to multi-channel OAM holography on a single phase profile. The metasurface is composed of subwavelength TiO2 nanopillar arrays with a fixed height of 600 nm on a SiO2 substrate. These nanopillars are designed as half-waveplates to convert the handedness of circular polarized (CP) light and impose a geometry phase when the nanopillars are rotated at various angles. Therefore, the final phase profile of the discontinuous OAM holography can be encoded pixel by pixel in the geometry-phase metasurface. Sample fabrication
The metasurface samples are prepared using electron beam lithography (EBL). Metasurfaces, composed of sub-wavelength artificial structure arrays, have made a profound impact on the fields of optics and photonics due to their exceptional performance, such as compact size and high resolution, ushering optical components into the era of planar optics. They possess unprecedented ability to manipulate various degrees of freedom, such as phase1–6, amplitude5,6, and polarization7,8, through intense light–matter interactions9–11. This capability enables metasurfaces to facilitate advanced multiplexing applications, particularly in metasurface holography, also referred to as meta-hologram12–14.

Recently, a variety of multiplexing techniques for metasurface holography have been explored, including polarization multiplexing15–17, wavelength multiplexing18–20, incident angle-multiplexing21–23, and spatial multiplexing24,25. Among these, orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing has emerged as an especially promising technique26–29, as OAM offers theoretically unlimited orthogonal channels. This enables the multiplexing of a large number of OAM-dependent information channels within a single meta-hologram30–40. However, conventional OAM-multiplexing holography relies on azimuthally symmetric OAM encoding. By randomly inputting regular OAM states, the encoded information can be easily retrieved, thereby significantly compromising the security of the information. The demonstration of a geometry-phase metasurface supporting the polarization-discontinuous OAM hybrid encoding is based on a non-interleaved method35. We integrated two-channel discontinuous OAM encoding with polarization multiplexing. When illuminated with an LCP beam carrying TC of l = ±15, the letter “M” is successfully decoded. For RCP beam illumination, four distinct images “1”, “2”, “3”, and “4” can likewise be decoded as shown in Fig. 5c, demonstrating polarization multiplexing capability.

The reconstructed images exhibit near-perfect Gaussian spot profiles. The polarization selectivity and azimuthal selectivity of discontinuous OAM ensure that each channel is activated only when the polarization and the alignment of the incident beam match the encoded phase profile, thereby enabling dynamic, high-capacity, and high-security holography with cryptographic robustness. Notably, the numerals and letters in all the holographic images shown in Figs. 3–5 are designed in the same spatial position, yet exhibit almost no crosstalk between different channels.

## Methods

Sample fabrication
The metasurface samples are prepared using electron beam lithography (EBL). First, a 600 nm-thick titanium dioxide (TiO2) film is deposited on a silicon dioxide (SiO2) substrate by sputtering evaporation. A polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) layer is evenly spin-coated onto the TiO2 film. After EBL, the PMMA resist is developed, and a Cr film is deposited on the PMMA using electron beam evaporation (EBE). The undeveloped PMMA is removed, and the TiO2 is etched using reactive ion etching. The process end with the removal of the Cr mask by chemical etching.

Optical setup
The experimental optical setup for the discontinuous OAM holography is shown in Fig. 2b. The laser from a supercontinuum laser source (SC-PRO, Wuhan Yangtze Soton Laser Co., Ltd., 430–2400 nm) filtered by an acousto-optic tunable filter (AOTF, Wuhan Yangtze Soton Laser Co., Ltd., 400–2000 nm) is initially expand the beam through the objective lens (L1, NA = 0.65) and then directed through a beam splitter, projected perpendicularly onto a spatial light modulator (SLM, HOLOEYE PLUTO-2.1-NIR−135, German). This is to generate a vertically emitted discontinuous OAM beam. Then, lens L2 (f = 150 mm), lens L3 (f = 50 mm), and lens L4 (f = 75 mm) are used to focus the discontinuous OAM onto the metasurface. A set of polarizer and quarter-wave plate is used to convert the polarization of the incident beam from linear polarization to LCP light. A scientific complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor camera (Dhyana 400BSI V2, Tucsen, China) is used to extract the holographic images.

Comment 2: This manuscript proposes a new paradigm of metasurface holography
based on discontinuous orbital angular momentum (OAM), which enables multi-
channel holographic encoding under a single incident beam by breaking the rotational
symmetry of conventional OAM modes. The work demonstrates certain innovation in
enhancing optical information security and capacity, particularly in the design and
application of spatially varying topological charge (TC) distributions. However,
considering the high academic standards and scientific rigor expected by Nature
Communications, the current manuscript still exhibits certain shortcomings in
theoretical depth, experimental validation, and practical feasibility, falling short of the
publication threshold. To improve the overall quality of the manuscript, the authors are
advised to systematically address the following key issues.
Response 2: We would like to thank the reviewer for the affirmation of the novelty of
our work. We are happy to address all the concerns raised by the reviewer.
Comment 2.1: First, traditional OAM multiplexing holography has shown great
potential in high-capacity communication due to its propagation-invariant and stable
characteristics. However, the proposed discontinuous OAM mode, while breaking the
central symmetry, may adversely affect the beam’s transmission properties. For
example, it remains insufficiently verified whether the structural integrity of the beam
can be preserved after transmission through optical fibers (such as few-mode or ring-
core fibers) or through free space. Therefore, the application prospects emphasized in
the manuscript require further substantiation, and it is recommended that the authors
supplement the manuscript with relevant experimental or simulation-based analyses of
transmission performance.
Response 2.1: The authors thank the reviewer for this point. Taking two-channel
discontinuous OAM as an example. Within the oresnel diffraction regime, a vortex
beam carrying half-integer OAM exhibits a semi-vortex morphology. The opening
direction of this semi-vortex rotates with propagation distance until attaining a 90°
phase offset relative to its initial state. The rotation direction is determined by the sign
of the TC as explained in Supplementary Note 2. The discontinuous OAM proposed
in this manuscript arises from the superposition of two such semi-vortices, which
generate a petal-like beam profile. After the oresnel diffraction regime, i.e., in the far
field, the discontinuous OAM beam propagates stable in free space as shown in Fig.
S21.
Fig. S21. The simulated propagation characteristics of the discontinuous OAM

Comment 2.2: Second, although the authors claim that the method effectively enhances
the capacity of encryption channels, the experimental results presented in the
manuscript demonstrate only a limited number of multiplexed channels—just a few in
total. In contrast, traditional OAM holography has already achieved tens or even
hundreds of multiplexed channels, with some metasurface-based schemes reaching
over ten channels. As such, the advantage of the current approach in terms of
capacity enhancement is not yet clearly demonstrated. The authors are encouraged to
more explicitly clarify the core competitiveness of their method compared to traditional
techniques and to further validate its potential by expanding the number of channels or
integrating additional degrees of freedom.
Response 2.2: The authors thank the reviewer for this valuable point. Conventional
OAM metasurface holography achieving tens or hundreds of multiplexed channels
relies on complex-amplitude metasurfaces. Compared to phase-only metasurfaces,
complex-amplitude designs exhibit lower crosstalk and higher image fidelity. However,
due to fabrication constraints in realizing complex-amplitude structures in our
laboratory, we adopted a phase-only metasurface approach utilizing Pancharatnam-
Berry (PB) phase for multi-channel multiplexing. In the previous paper presented by
Ren Haoran et al. (Nat. Commun., 10, 2986, 2019), they demonstrated ten-channel
phase-only OAM holography in simulations. oor comparison, we present both
simulation and experimental results for ten-channel discontinuous OAM holography.
In Fig. S17 and Fig. S18, we show that both eight-channel and ten-channel
discontinuous OAM holography can be successfully achieved.
The key advantage over discontinuous OAM holography lies in enabling channel
switching through metasurface rotation under single-beam illumination, which is an
unattainable feature in traditional systems. Moreover, it offers enhanced security as
decoding requires precise knowledge of both the encoded azimuthal sectors and their
corresponding TC.

Comment 2.3: Third, although conventional centrally symmetric OAM multiplexing
holography imposes certain alignment requirements on the devices, its inherent
symmetry to some extent reduces the difficulty of alignment. After breaking this
symmetry, however, the precision required for alignment may significantly increase,
especially when rotational operations are introduced, where accurate centering
becomes critical to decoding performance. The manuscript should therefore include a
discussion on alignment error tolerance and assess its impact on overall system
performance.
Response 2.3: The authors thank the reviewer for this point. In contrast to conventional
OAM holography, our proposed discontinuous OAM holography requires angular
alignment—a deliberate design feature that enhances information security. Random
illumination with integer-OAM modes cannot decode the information, while the system
maintains robust tolerance to both angular misalignment and center-position offsets.
The discussion has been added in Supplementary Note 7.

lateral misalignment in discontinuous OAM holography.
Our investigation into the effects of angular and lateral misalignment in
discontinuous OAM holography reveals important operational characteristics of this
technique. Using a four-channel discontinuous OAM hologram as an example, we find

deviation.

discontinuous OAM in resisting spiral spectrum analysis, it lacks thorough security
analysis under more complex attack scenarios, such as phase reconstruction based on
machine learning or partial information leakage. It is recommended that the authors
supplement the manuscript with corresponding experimental or simulation data to
verify the system’s robustness under different attack models and explore potential
mechanisms for enhancing security.

valuable insights for our research. Indeed, there are some related researches using deep
learning to recover the conventional holography (such as Opt. Commun., 529(15),

optics, holography, cryptographic imaging, and multifunctional metasurface design.

publication in Nature Communications after minor revision.

## Paper

## Abstract

Orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing holography has emerged as a pivotal technology for high-capacity optical communication, encryption and display, but it requires multiple inputs for decoding and its security remains constrained due to the rotational symmetry of topological charge (TC) distribution in conventional OAM modes. Here, we introduce a general paradigm of OAM multiplexing holography that enables multi-channel holographic encoding using a single incident light. Our methodology leverages a discontinuous OAM with a spatially varying TC across the azimuth, which breaks the rotational symmetry and imposes angular selectivity for information retrieval. Notably, by rationally designing the TC distribution, the discontinuous OAM exhibits self-orthogonality at different rotation angles, laying the foundation for multiplexed holography. A modified weighted Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm is developed to calculate the holographic phase profile, which can then be encoded onto a pure geometry-phase metasurface. By further integrating different pairs of discontinuous OAMs, we successfully expand the channel capacity for holographic multiplexing, significantly advancing high-security and high-capacity optical information encryption. Our work establishes discontinuous OAM as a versatile platform for secure optical communications, high-density data storage, and dynamic holographic displays, bridging the gap between structured light manipulation and cryptographic robustness.

---

## Introduction

Metasurfaces, composed of sub-wavelength artificial structure arrays, have made a profound impact on the fields of optics and photonics due to their exceptional performance, such as compact size and high resolution, ushering optical components into the era of planar optics. They possess unprecedented ability to manipulate various degrees of freedom, such as phase1–6, amplitude5,6, and polarization7,8, through intense light–matter interactions9–11. This capability enables metasurfaces to facilitate advanced multiplexing applications, particularly in metasurface holography, also referred to as meta-hologram12–14.

Recently, a variety of multiplexing techniques for metasurface holography have been explored, including polarization multiplexing15–17, wavelength multiplexing18–20, incident angle-multiplexing21–23, and spatial multiplexing24,25. Among these, orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing has emerged as an especially promising technique26–29, as OAM offers theoretically unlimited orthogonal channels. This enables the multiplexing of a large number of OAM-dependent information channels within a single meta-hologram30–40. However, conventional OAM-multiplexing holography relies on azimuthally symmetric OAM encoding. By randomly inputting regular OAM states, the encoded information can be easily retrieved, thereby significantly compromising the security of the information. In addition, each channel is encoded with a single constant topological charge (TC) of OAM, which inevitably requires different input vortex beams with distinct TCs of OAM to decode separate holographic images, thereby complicating the generation of multiple holographic channels.

Here, we propose a general method for OAM multiplexing holography using a single input beam that is azimuthally encoded with discontinuous TCs of OAM. Our methodology relies on the fact that the discontinuous arrangement of TC breaks the rotational symmetry of the OAM mode, laying the foundation to encode multiple holographic channels by simply rotating the single input beam. We prove that by strategically arranging the azimuthally distributed TCs, the discontinuous OAM exhibits self-orthogonality at different rotation angles, ensuring minimal cross-talk between channels. Additionally, various discontinuous OAMs can be multiplexed on a single device, further enhancing the holographic channels. To achieve this, a modified weighted Gerchberg–Saxton (WGS) algorithm is introduced for the generation of holographic phase information, which is then encoded in a pure geometry-phase metasurface. Notably, the encrypted holographic images using the discontinuous OAM cannot be decrypted by illuminating with conventional continuous OAM, significantly enhancing the security of the information. Our work paves the way for high-capacity and high-security information transfer and optical networks, addressing the escalating demands of optical and quantum communications, as well as big-data photonics.

---

## Results

Design principle of discontinuous OAM holography
The design principle of discontinuous OAM metasurface holography is illustrated in Fig. 1. In conventional OAM holography, the illuminated OAM mode exhibits rotational symmetry due to the constant TC, resulting in an output holographic image that remains invariant regardless of the incident beam’s rotation angle as shown in Fig. 1a. In contrast, the proposed discontinuous OAM holography leverages a rotational symmetry broken OAM mode, featuring azimuthally encoded TCs, which exhibit azimuth-dependent channel selectivity as shown in Fig. 1b. The encoded holographic image can only be reconstructed when the azimuth of the incident OAM mode aligns precisely with the encoded phase. This enables multiple holographic images to be encoded at different rotation angles of the incident OAM mode, significantly enhancing the multiplexing channel numbers under single beam illumination. Our discontinuous OAM holography offers a security enhancement of at least 7 orders of magnitude compared to traditional OAM holographic encryption (see more details in Supplementary Note 1). Specifically, we encode distinct TCs across varying azimuth, with each TC value assigned to a specific angular region defined as l(θ). Switching between multiple independent channels—from image “A” to “D”—can be achieved by rotating the input OAM mode. Compared to constant OAM, discontinuous OAM generates multimodal spectral interference due to its azimuthal phase partitioning. This inherent complexity fundamentally resists detection and decryption through spiral spectrum analysis. Consequently, any attempt to reconstruct the encrypted hologram via exhaustive constant OAM modes fails to achieve meaningful reconstruction.

To investigate the optical properties of discontinuous OAM, we design a dual-partition OAM by evenly dividing the azimuth into two regions, each encoded with distinct TCs. Generally, the electric field distribution of the output beam by illuminating the discontinuous OAM can be expressed as41,

E(r,ϕ) = C \sum_{j=-1}^{0} a_j e^{i(l+j)(ϕ∓π/2)} \int J_{l+j}(krρ/f) ρ dρ (1)

where i^2 = −1, r and ϕ are the polar coordinates on the output image plane, ρ is the radial coordinates on the metasurface plane, f is the focal length, λ is the operating wavelength, k = 2π/λ is the wave-vector, a_j is the coefficient related to the rectangular function, l denotes the number of TC, J(·) is the Bessel function, C is a constant.

In the example illustrated in Fig. 1c, the azimuthal plane is divided into two distinct regions (top-left panel of Fig. 1c: the brown segment encodes a negative TC of l = −10, while the blue segment encodes a positive TC of l = 10). The electric field distribution of the output light undergoes a characteristic 90° rotation relative to the encoded phase pattern (bottom-left panel of Fig. 1c), with the rotation direction governed by the sign of TC (see more details of the rotation rules in Supplementary Note 2 and Fig. S2). Specifically, a negative TC induces a −90° rotation of the spatial electric field distribution, whereas a positive TC generates a +90° rotation. Therefore, for the dual-partition discontinuous OAM with opposite sign of TCs, the spatial electric field distributions of the two partitioned regions overlap coherently in free space as shown in the bottom-left panel of Fig. 1c, which can be described as,

E ∝ cos(10ϕ), ϕ ∈ [π/2, 3π/2] (2)

However, the phase discontinuity between the two regions and the mismatch in TC at the partitioned boundaries introduce a half-period gap in the petal pattern, breaking the rotational symmetry and resulting in an asymmetric intensity profile.

We further investigate the self-orthogonality of the discontinuous OAM mode at different rotation angles. As illustrated in Fig. 1c, d, two sets of multiplexing configurations with different relative rotation angles—Multiplexing Mode 1 and Multiplexing Mode 2 are analyzed. In Mode 1, the two discontinuous OAMs (first two columns of Fig. 1c) exhibit a relative rotation angle of 180°, showing no overlap in their azimuthal TC distribution, thereby ensuring complete orthogonality. This orthogonality is also manifested in real space as the beam propagates (bottom panel of Fig. 1c). Each discontinuous OAM contributes symmetrically to half of the ring pattern, and their superposition yields a uniform annular intensity profile. In contrast, Mode 2 introduces a 90° azimuthal shift between the two OAMs, showing partial overlap of the TC distribution (red dashed box in the top panel of Fig. 1d), which leads to crosstalk in the spatial electric field distributions. This overlap breaks orthogonality, and the superposition in real space generates an interference pattern with crosstalk. Figure 1e quantifies the orthogonality of the two modes (see calculation details in Supplementary Notes 3 and 4), highlighting the superior orthogonality of Mode 1 compared to Mode 2. As a result, Mode 1 is suitable for multiplexing due to its complete orthogonality. These findings underscore the critical role of spatially non-overlapping discontinuous OAM designs in achieving high-fidelity multiplexing holography.

Design processes of discontinuous OAM holography
The algorithm process for the discontinuous OAM multiplexing holography is shown in Fig. 2a. The holographic phase information for different channels is first generated from sampled images using a WGS algorithm (see details in Supplementary Note 5). The phase is subsequently superimposed with the discontinuous OAM at different rotation angles. The final phase profile is obtained by superimposing all holographic channels, leading to multi-channel OAM holography on a single phase profile. The metasurface is composed of subwavelength TiO2 nanopillar arrays with a fixed height of 600 nm on a SiO2 substrate. These nanopillars are designed as half-waveplates to convert the handedness of circular polarized (CP) light and impose a geometry phase when the nanopillars are rotated at various angles. Therefore, the final phase profile of the discontinuous OAM holography can be encoded pixel by pixel in the geometry-phase metasurface. The width and length of the nanopillars are chosen as L1 = 100 nm and L2 = 290 nm, showing optimized CP conversion efficiency in the visible range (see more details in Supplementary Note 6). The experimental optical setup (see more details in the “Methods” section) and the scanning electron microscopic image of the fabricated metasurface are illustrated in Fig. 2b, c, respectively.

Experiments of single-discontinuous-OAM multiplexing holography
Figure 3a, b show the decoded holograms of two discontinuous OAM multiplexing modes, with simulation results in the second row and experimental results in the third row. In Mode 1, when two discontinuous OAM beams with rotation angles of 0° and 180° are illuminated, a minimal crosstalk between the two images is observed due to their complete orthogonality as discussed in Fig. 1c, and near-perfect Gaussian spot distribution are obtained as shown in the first two columns of Fig. 3a. It should be noted that slight crosstalk between the two channels appears in the experimental results due to fabrication errors. When illuminated by a plane wave, as shown in the third column of Fig. 3a, the two images of “0” and “1” do not overlap, each showing opposite half-ring vortices (see the zoomed-in figures in the bottom-right panel of Fig. 3a): Image “0” shows a right-half vortex, while Image “1” shows a left-half vortex, with their opening directions matching those in Fig. 1c. The overlapping regions of Image “0” and “1” produce a seamless annular “petal-like” intensity profile formed by their coherent superposition. In contrast, Mode 2, with a relative rotation angle of 90° between the two discontinuous incident OAMs, suffers from non-orthogonality as discussed in Fig. 1d, leading to significant crosstalk that degrades image quality as shown in the first two columns of Fig. 3b. Although the decoded images still yield a Gaussian-like spot distribution, the non-overlapping regions for Image “0” retain the right-half vortex, while Image “1” displays a top-half vortex. As a result, under plane wave illumination, the overlapping regions generate an incomplete three-quarter annular pattern.

To quantify the imaging fidelity, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is calculated for both modes as shown in Fig. 3c. It is evident that Mode 1 achieves a higher SNR than Mode 2. Figure 3d further demonstrates the azimuth sensitivity of discontinuous OAM. Rotating the incident beam reduces the SNR of the original channel while progressively activating the complementary channel (see more details in Supplementary Note 4). Specifically, at a 0° rotation, Image “0” is fully decoded, while at a 180° rotation, Image “1” is fully decoded, highlighting the rotation-angle selectivity of the incident beam inherent in the discontinuous OAM encoding. This behavior underscores the multidimensional security and dynamic channel-switching capabilities enabled by discontinuous OAM holography.

To validate the scalability of our method, a four-channel discontinuous OAM holography is designed as shown in Fig. 4, where distinct information channels are selectively activated by rotating the incident discontinuous OAM beam with 90° intervals. Figure 4a illustrates the rotational encoding scheme, and Fig. 4b quantifies the SNR of the decoded images across the four channels as a function of rotation angle. At 0°, 90°, 180°, and 270° rotations, the SNR of the decoded images “A”, “B”, “C”, and “D” are normalized to 1, respectively, with the maximal SNR occurring at these angles, while intermediate angles exhibit severe crosstalk. Both simulated (Fig. 4c) and experimental results (Fig. 4d) confirm the azimuth selectivity. The reconstructed patterns at intermediate angles, characterized by hybrid intensity profiles, are detailed in Supplementary Note 7.

Experiments of multiple polarization and discontinuous-OAM hybrid multiplexing holography
To further expand multiplexing dimensions and enhance channel capacity, we incorporated polarization and multiple pairs of discontinuous OAMs as an additional degree of freedom. Specifically, by integrating two pairs of discontinuous OAM modes with two orthogonal polarization states, we have designed an eight-channel metasurface multiplexed holography in Fig. 5. For left-circularly polarized (LCP) light, two pairs of orthogonal discontinuous OAM modes l = ±15, l = ±22 are employed to encode four distinct images. Similarly, for right-circularly polarized (RCP) light, the set of OAM modes l = ±15, l = ±10 encodes another four independent images. The superimposed phase of LCP light denoted by σ+ is inverted due to the opposite phase response between RCP and LCP, as shown in Fig. 5a. Consequently, the phase profile can be expressed as,

φ = arg [\sum_{n=1}^{N} e^{i(φ_n^{σ-} + ϕ_n^{r1})} + \sum_{m=1}^{M} e^{i(φ_m^{σ+} + ϕ_m^{r2})}] (3)

where channel n = 1, 2, ..., N, with N being the channel number of discontinuous OAM holography for RCP, m = 1, 2, ..., M, with M being the channel number of discontinuous OAM holography for LCP, σ- and σ+ denote RCP and LCP, respectively, φ_n^σ and φ_m^σ is the calculated phase by the WGS algorithm. The phase of discontinuous OAM ϕ_n^r1 and ϕ_n^r2 is then added to the holographic phase.

The demonstration of a geometry-phase metasurface supporting the polarization-discontinuous OAM hybrid encoding is based on a non-interleaved method35. We integrated two-channel discontinuous OAM encoding with polarization multiplexing. When illuminated with an LCP beam carrying TC of l = ±15, the letter “M” is successfully decoded. When the metasurface is rotated by 180°, the decoded image switches from letter “M” to letter “E”, demonstrating dynamic channel switching through angular control as shown in Fig. 5b. Similarly, when illuminated with LCP beam carrying l = ±22, the letter “T” is decoded, and a 180° rotation of the metasurface enables switching from “T” to “A”. For RCP beam illumination, four distinct images “1”, “2”, “3”, and “4” can likewise be decoded as shown in Fig. 5c, demonstrating polarization multiplexing capability.

The reconstructed images exhibit near-perfect Gaussian spot profiles. The polarization selectivity and azimuthal selectivity of discontinuous OAM ensure that each channel is activated only when the polarization and the alignment of the incident beam match the encoded phase profile, thereby enabling dynamic, high-capacity, and high-security holography with cryptographic robustness. Notably, the numerals and letters in all the holographic images shown in Figs. 3–5 are designed in the same spatial position, yet exhibit almost no crosstalk between different channels.

## Methods

Sample fabrication
The metasurface samples are prepared using electron beam lithography (EBL). First, a 600 nm-thick titanium dioxide (TiO2) film is deposited on a silicon dioxide (SiO2) substrate by sputtering evaporation. A polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) layer is evenly spin-coated onto the TiO2 film. After EBL, the PMMA resist is developed, and a Cr film is deposited on the PMMA using electron beam evaporation (EBE). The undeveloped PMMA is removed, and the TiO2 is etched using reactive ion etching. The process end with the removal of the Cr mask by chemical etching.

Optical setup
The experimental optical setup for the discontinuous OAM holography is shown in Fig. 2b. The laser from a supercontinuum laser source (SC-PRO, Wuhan Yangtze Soton Laser Co., Ltd., 430–2400 nm) filtered by an acousto-optic tunable filter (AOTF, Wuhan Yangtze Soton Laser Co., Ltd., 400–2000 nm) is initially expand the beam through the objective lens (L1, NA = 0.65) and then directed through a beam splitter, projected perpendicularly onto a spatial light modulator (SLM, HOLOEYE PLUTO-2.1-NIR−135, German). This is to generate a vertically emitted discontinuous OAM beam. Then, lens L2 (f = 150 mm), lens L3 (f = 50 mm), and lens L4 (f = 75 mm) are used to focus the discontinuous OAM onto the metasurface. A set of polarizer and quarter-wave plate is used to convert the polarization of the incident beam from linear polarization to LCP light. A scientific complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor camera (Dhyana 400BSI V2, Tucsen, China) is used to extract the holographic images.
